candidateRows: Moral knowledge is impossible because no moral claim can receive evidential support sufficient for justified belief.
This states the con side's principal epistemological thesis and directly addresses the motion's question about justified moral knowledge.
After defining moral error theory, Lutz introduces moral skepticism as his second basic position and denies moral evidence, justification, and knowledge.
Moral facts would require desire-independent categorical reasons, but only desire-dependent reasons intelligibly rationalize action, so moral facts do not exist.
The argument supplies the central metaphysical route from a desire-based account of reasons to denial of objective moral facts.
Lutz defines categorical normativity, contrasts it with ordinary desire-based practical reasons, and argues that morality's required kind of reason is too strange to exist.
Evidence supports a belief only through best-explanation relations to experience, and moral truth is unnecessary to explain moral experience, so moral evidence and knowledge are unavailable.
This is the con side's central argument against the appearance-based justification and moral knowledge expressly raised by the motion.
Lutz presents explanationism, illustrates it with perceptual belief, then argues that naturalistic explanations of moral intuitions leave moral propositions without evidential work.
Error theory is less initially plausible than clear moral judgments such as the badness of suffering, while its desire-based premise lacks comparable intuitive force.
Huemer directly defends objective value by comparing the credibility of core moral appearances with the premises offered for anti-realism.
Lutz's opening contention that objective moral values do not exist because reasons must depend on desires.
Huemer distinguishes forms of anti-realism, identifies implications he regards as implausible, and argues that familiar moral judgments are more credible than anti-realist premises.
Appearances provide prima facie justification unless defeated, because denying all such justificatory force would leave the denial itself unjustified.
This gives the pro side's foundational answer to whether moral knowledge may be justified by appearances rather than explanatory inference alone.
Lutz's explanationist claim that justification arises only when a belief best explains experiential evidence.
Huemer states a defeasible appearance principle and supports it with a self-defeat argument directed against epistemologies that deny appearances any default justificatory role.
Cases involving imprudent students and preference reversal show that desire-based accounts cannot explain practical reasons without evaluative facts.
The examples attack the crucial desire-dependence premise supporting Lutz's metaphysical argument against objective moral facts.
Lutz's premise that every practical reason derives from an agent's desires, goals, or values.
Huemer reconstructs the Humean argument, uses a partying student and the sirens case to expose conflicting treatments of future desires, and invokes evaluative judgments to explain the difference.
Idealizing desires through vivid imagination cannot ground rational choice consistently, because imagination appropriately changes some choices but irrationally distorts others.
It blocks an important idealized-desire repair to the con side's central theory and supports the need for independent evaluative judgment.
A possible Humean repair that bases reasons on desires formed after vividly imagining consequences.
Huemer contrasts charitable concern produced by vivid imagination with medically harmful surgery avoidance produced by the same procedure, arguing that evaluation explains their difference.
Consistency has rational significance for value judgments only if they can be true or false, so error theory cannot preserve a reason to make values coherent.
The argument challenges error theory's ability to retain standards of rational consistency while denying truth-bearing evaluative facts.
The error-theoretic proposal that subjective desires or values can remain rationally organized without objective value facts.
Huemer contrasts beliefs, whose inconsistency guarantees falsity, with desires, which need not correspond to reality, and argues that facts are needed to explain concern for consistency.
The dispute between realism and a Humean theory of reasons cannot be settled by simply reversing the conditional; competing positions must be assessed as broader worldviews.
This answers Huemer's realism-based rejection of the Humean premise and explains Lutz's proposed basis for adjudicating the central theoretical impasse.
Huemer's objection that the Humean theory should be rejected because it conflicts with independently credible moral realism.
Lutz characterizes the opposing inferences as a logical standoff and argues that each theory belongs within a wider package concerning morality, epistemology, and metaphysics.
Counterexamples involving overpowering desires refute proportionalism, not desire-based reasons, because normative weight can depend on a desire's centrality to the agent's self-conception.
This directly repairs the desire-based theory against Huemer's strongest practical counterexamples while preserving the premise underwriting moral anti-realism.
Huemer's student and sirens cases offered to show that desire-based theories yield incorrect judgments about practical reasons.

Lutz separates motivational strength from normative weight, rejects proportionalism, and proposes that reasons track desires central to an agent's identity, applying the account to students and the sirens case.
The extreme moral consequences of error theory are initially less plausible than the desire-based theory from which they follow.
This directly challenges moral error theory by comparing the credibility of its denial of paradigmatic moral wrongs with that of its supporting theory of reasons.
Lutz's preceding defense of a desire-based account of normative reasons.
After Lutz develops a non-proportional desire account, Huemer restores the central dispute by arguing that confidence in obvious moral wrongs should outweigh confidence in that account.
Centrality to self-conception does not explain rational priority, because ordinary weakness-of-will cases turn on judgments of what is better.
The move attacks the principal revision Lutz uses to preserve desire-based reasons while avoiding the counterexamples facing simple proportionalism.
Lutz's claim that a desire's normative strength depends on its centrality to the agent's self-conception.
Huemer uses delayed gratification, the partying student, and a person who identifies as irrational to argue that evaluative judgment, not identity centrality, explains rational choice.
Rational reflection can distinguish momentarily forceful alien desires from desires rooted more deeply in an agent's deliberative self.
This is Lutz's main defense of a non-proportional desire theory against weakness-of-will and compulsion cases that otherwise threaten the theory.
Huemer's and the moderator's objections that self-centrality is vague, arbitrary, and insufficiently grounded.
Lutz concedes that centrality needs refinement but argues that deliberative agents can criticize powerful compulsions by reference to a deeper practical identity and perspective.
Invoking self-centrality either lacks a desire-based explanation of its authority or covertly treats centrality as intrinsically normative.
The objection alleges that Lutz's proposed standard cannot remain wholly internal to a Humean theory and therefore threatens the coherence of his central defense.
Lutz's appeal to deeper selfhood as the source of rational authority over motivationally stronger desires.
Huemer argues that the authority of self-centrality must itself derive from desire to remain Humean, then adds that all desires arise from unchosen biological or cultural sources.
Reasons must resonate with an agent's values and deliberative perspective, because wholly disconnected demands would be alienating and lack practical purchase.
This supplies the theoretical foundation requested for the self-centrality account and connects the theory of reasons to the broader error-theoretic worldview.
Huemer's request for a theoretical explanation of why differences among an agent's desires normatively matter.
Lutz invokes internal reasons and alienation to argue that rational action must connect with the goals, values, and desires structuring the perspective from which an agent deliberates.
Abandoning belief in moral facts would make ordinary conduct more selfish because moral judgments help generate and organize people's practical desires.
The move argues that objective moral belief has significant practical consequences, directly contesting the error theorist's account of how moral thought relates to action.
Lutz's claim that people would continue pursuing what seems worthy even if they accepted that no moral facts exist.
Huemer predicts reduced charitable and cooperative behavior without moral realism and explains that many desires are intertwined with judgments about rightness, loyalty, and value.
Moral beliefs commonly project antecedent values onto the world, so removing the objective belief need not remove the attitudes that motivate conduct.
This explains both why pervasive moral belief can exist without moral facts and why accepting error theory need not radically alter most people's behavior.
Huemer's contention that losing objective moral beliefs would substantially alter desires, emotions, and morally guided behavior.
Lutz argues that values and emotions generate an illusory objective overlay; most agents would retain the underlying concern and behavior, while purely duty-driven agents are atypical.
Moral judgment can guide action independently of emotional appeal, and rejecting moral facts can consequently transform both emotion and motivation.
The move disputes Lutz's psychological separation of attitudes from objective moral belief and supports the claim that realism materially affects deliberation and conduct.
Lutz's projective account according to which underlying values and emotions generally survive the abandonment of objective moral belief.
Huemer uses emotionally unappealing charitable choices and third-party injustice to argue that evaluative judgments shape feelings and intervention, rather than merely overlaying prior attitudes.
Psychological evidence indicates that emotions usually drive moral judgments, while apparently unemotional deliberation still rests on stable cold passions.
This empirical and motivational reply supports the error theorist's claim that abandoning objective moral beliefs usually leaves practical commitments intact.
Huemer's claim that moral beliefs commonly produce or reshape the emotions and desires responsible for action.
Lutz argues that affect generally precedes moral judgment and treats calm intellectual commitments as long-standing passions that remain connected to an agent's self-conception.
Social-intuitionist findings from unusual cases do not establish general emotional priority, and undermining a judgment can also undermine its associated emotion.
The response challenges the empirical support for Lutz's causal model and argues that belief revision can still change emotion, motivation, and behavior.
Lutz's appeal to social-intuitionist evidence and cold passions as support for emotion-driven moral judgment.

Huemer questions generalization from unusual experimental prompts, proposes unconscious cognition behind emotion, and explains how recognizing a judgment as false can correct anger and subsequent action.
Experiences justify ordinary perceptual beliefs through causal background models, not by intrinsically possessing propositional content.
This supplies the principal explanationist alternative to phenomenal conservatism and directly bears on whether appearances can provide immediate justification.
Huemer's view that an experience with propositional content provides prima facie justification for its content.
After the moderator frames the dispute between explanationism and intuitionism, Lutz accepts experience as epistemically important but gives its justificatory role a causal interpretation.
Explanationism ultimately presupposes an initial entitlement to accept appearances, because concepts, causal beliefs, and explanatory judgments cannot otherwise get started.
The argument attacks the foundations of the rival epistemology and supports the motion's claim that appearances can justify beliefs independently of best-explanation evidence.
Lutz's claim that perceptual justification arises from causal background beliefs rather than propositional experiential content.

Huemer first clarifies experiential content, then argues that representation is required for acquiring concepts and that explanationist background beliefs themselves trace back to accepted appearances.
Predictive refinement can generate sophisticated conceptual and causal models without beginning from contentful experiences accepted as foundationally true.
This is Lutz's main rebuttal to the alleged regress in explanationism, offering a mechanism by which cognition can develop without Huemer's foundational appearances.
Huemer's contention that causal and explanatory cognition must begin by accepting contentful appearances as accurate.
Lutz invokes learning in artificial systems and predictive-processing accounts of brains to argue that reliable conceptual structure can emerge through prediction-driven refinement.
Once genuine mental representation arises, perceptual concepts and beliefs still derive from prior experiences that represent worldly objects.
The move preserves Huemer's foundational argument by distinguishing merely interpreted computer data from genuine mental content and concept acquisition.
Lutz's predictive-processing analogy suggesting that conceptual structure can emerge without prior contentful experience.
Huemer denies that computers possess intrinsic representation, allows that infant cognition may initially lack it, and argues that mature perceptual concepts depend on representational experiences.
The AI analogy concerns the functional emergence of conceptual distinctions, and supports the possibility that concepts arise through predictive refinement without prior contentful experience.
This clarification protects the explanatory force of Lutz's predictive model from Huemer's objection that computers lack genuine mental states or intrinsic representation.
Huemer's objection that computers have no genuine mental states and represent only through human interpretation.
Lutz narrows the analogy to functional learning, cites predictive refinement in brains, and argues that conceptual discrimination need not be preceded by content-bearing experience.
Mathematical seeming is evidence that a thinker is correctly applying interrelated concepts, rather than an intellectual appearance whose content is the mathematical proposition itself.
The move extends explanationism to a priori knowledge, addressing a major proposed counterexample to the claim that justification depends on explanatory evidence.
The intuitionist challenge that the powerful seeming of elementary mathematical truths directly justifies believing them.
Lutz acknowledges experiences during mathematical reflection but interprets their associated confidence as evidence about conceptual relations discoverable through reflective inquiry.
Necessary truths such as the incompatibility of being wholly red and wholly blue appear synthetic a priori because synonym substitution does not reduce them to logical truths.
This supplies a concrete counterexample to Lutz's treatment of a priori knowledge and supports Huemer's broader rationalist epistemology underlying moral intuitionism.
Lutz's empiricist proposal that mathematical and other a priori truths are conceptual or analytic truths.
Huemer invokes a traditional criterion of analyticity, argues that color incompatibility cannot be derived by replacing terms with synonyms, and points to similar metaphysical cases.
Color incompatibility is analytic in a broad conceptual sense because understanding phenomenal color concepts reveals that being wholly red and wholly blue are inconsistent.
The response aims to absorb Huemer's proposed synthetic a priori counterexample into empiricism and thereby defend Lutz's explanationist epistemological framework.
Huemer's argument that red-blue incompatibility is a synthetic a priori truth not reducible through synonym substitution.
Lutz adopts a broader notion of analyticity grounded in phenomenal-concept mastery, while conceding that he has not yet produced a fully worked-out general account.
Both debaters reject reductive ethical naturalism, but moral error theory follows only if every justified belief must explain observations, a requirement Huemer denies.
This isolates the central inferential divide determining whether the failure of naturalist moral explanations supports rejecting morality or leaves non-explanatory justification available.
Lutz's inference from the explanatory failure of ethical naturalism and his requirement that justified beliefs explain observations.
In closing, Huemer says both sides agree that identifying moral properties with natural properties explains no observations, then locates their disagreement in explanationism itself.
A priori knowledge concerns the natures of objects rather than merely words or concepts, and understanding badness and suffering can therefore reveal that suffering is bad.
The move connects the dispute over a priori knowledge directly to moral realism by presenting moral appearances as insight into objective relations among suffering and badness.
Lutz's broad analytic account of color incompatibility and his claim that reflective experience discloses relations among concepts.
Huemer argues that calling red and blue incompatible risks reducing analyticity to necessity, then proposes knowledge of objective natures and extends that model to the badness of suffering.
